arXiv:2611.17091v1 [cs.CL] 12 Nov 2026

Optimal Single-History Tokenization Disambiguation
for Provably Secure Linguistic Steganography

Feng Jiang Affiliation: School of Cyberspace, Hangzhou Dianzi University Email: fengjiang@hdu.edu.cn
Abstract

Provably secure linguistic steganography assumes that the receiver recovers the sender’s tokens, but a text channel delivers only text, and ambiguous tokenizations break extraction. Existing fixes change the distribution, synchronize whole pools of tokens at a capacity that collapses with large vocabularies, or track several token histories. We prove that if extraction is exact and error-free across full-support language models, a single-history receiver is confined to a prefix-free candidate set at every step—even if it reads the entire future text and the sender constrains later steps—and must therefore give up the stop entropy, the entropy of deciding whether each prefix token ends there. Fixing these stop decisions on the prefix forest with shared randomness yields coin projection: a closed-form scheme that attains the bound, works with any distribution coder in one model call per token, preserves ordinary sampling, and refines SyncPool for every key. Across English, Chinese and Japanese, ambiguous text is rare (at most 11 in 1,000 tokens), yet the stop entropy at word and morpheme prefixes takes 7.2–9.0% of the entropy at every step; SyncPool’s further loss comes from space and single-byte UTF-8 hubs that merge subtrees while carrying almost no stop uncertainty. Coin projection keeps 91–93% of the string entropy for the coder at every vocabulary size; with the full vocabulary, it turns 2.16–6.85 times as much entropy into message bits as SyncPool and recovers every completed message.

1 Introduction

Provably secure linguistic steganography hides a message in text sampled from a language model. The stegotext then follows the model’s own distribution, and no warden without the key can tell it from ordinary output (Hopper et al., 2002; Ziegler et al., 2019; Kaptchuk et al., 2021; de Witt et al., 2023; Ding et al., 2023). The coders behind these schemes assume that the receiver recovers the sender’s tokens. Real channels carry text, however, and one text admits many tokenizations. When the receiver retokenizes, it can recover a different sequence; with 7B models, 5–10% of 128-bit messages are lost (Yan and Murawaki, 2025).

Existing fixes pay for disambiguation in one of three ways. Filters remove candidates so that the text parses uniquely (Nozaki and Murawaki, 2022; Yan et al., 2023; Yan and Murawaki, 2025). They thereby change the distribution that security rests on. SyncPool keeps the distribution exact by encoding pools of prefix-related tokens (Qi et al., 2025). A single short token, however, can be a byte prefix of most candidates; the bare space is a prefix of nearly every English word token. The pools then merge, and capacity collapses as the vocabulary grows. On Llama-3.2 with the full vocabulary, SyncPool’s coder sees only 14% of the entropy (Section 3). Multi-history schemes recover nearly all the entropy, but they call the model on several tokenizations at every step (Feng et al., 2025).

We ask how much capacity an exact, zero-error scheme must give up when the receiver keeps a single token history, as SyncPool and standard decoders do. The answer is exactly the stop entropy HstopH_{\mathrm{stop}}. This is the entropy of deciding, at every candidate that is a byte prefix of other candidates, whether the token ends there. Figure 1 shows this cost on one step of a real model.

Our contributions are as follows.

  • •

    A tight single-history bound. Across full-support language models, any exact, error-free scheme with a single-history receiver is confined to prefix-free candidate sets at every step—even if the receiver reads the whole text and the sender constrains later steps—and embeds at most Hstr−HstopH_{\mathrm{str}}-H_{\mathrm{stop}} bits per step; reaching equality allows randomizing only end-of-token decisions (Theorems 1 and 2).

  • •

    Coin projection. Realizing those stop decisions on the prefix forest gives a closed-form scheme that attains the bound, works with any distribution coder in one model call per token, keeps the law of ordinary sampling, and refines SyncPool for every key (Section 4.1).

  • •

    Orthographic hubs versus lexical prefixes. Although at most 11 tokens in 1,000 are tokenized non-canonically, HstopH_{\mathrm{stop}} stays at 7.2–9.0% of the entropy across scripts and vocabulary sizes because it comes from complete words, stems and particles that can either stand alone or take a continuation; the bare space and single-byte UTF-8 prefixes merge whole subtrees yet rarely end a token, inflating only the branch entropy that SyncPool gives up (Section 3). Among the evaluated single-history methods on three languages, only coin projection is exact, recovers every completed message, and leaves over 90% of the string entropy to the coder at every vocabulary size (Section 5).

2 Background

Provably secure steganography.

Sender and receiver share a secret key KK and a context. At step tt, the language model gives a token law πt\pi_{t} on the history, truncated to the top kk tokens for a public kk. A distribution coder takes a law PP over a finite alphabet, the state of the message, and pseudo-random bits derived from KK, and outputs a symbol. Over the key, the symbol follows PP exactly. Given PP and the symbol, the receiver updates its knowledge of the message. Arithmetic coding (Ziegler et al., 2019), Meteor (Kaptchuk et al., 2021), iMEC (de Witt et al., 2023), Discop (Ding et al., 2023), Shimmer (Bai et al., 2025), SparSamp (Wang et al., 2025) and range coding (Yan and Murawaki, 2026) all fit this interface and embed up to H⁡(P)H(P) bits per step. If P=πtP=\pi_{t} at every step, the stegotext follows ordinary sampling, so no warden without the key can tell it from cover text (Hopper et al., 2002; Cachin, 1998).

The text channel.

These coders assume that the receiver knows every token. A text channel delivers only the text. Each token xx spells a nonempty byte string β⁡(x)\beta(x), and different token sequences can spell the same text. When the receiver retokenizes the text, it may therefore recover a sequence other than the one the sender emitted. Its coder inputs then differ from the sender’s: the message is lost.

There are two sources of ambiguity. The first is prefixes: when both ␣a and ␣an are candidates, a text that continues with ␣an can be read either way. The second is homographs, distinct tokens that spell the same string, which no text-only receiver can tell apart. We write p(v)=∑x:β⁡(x)=vπt(x)p(v)=\sum_{x:\,\beta(x)=v}\pi_{t}(x) for the string law. Its entropy is Hstr=H⁡(p)H_{\mathrm{str}}=H(p), and Htok=H⁡(πt)=Hstr+HhomH_{\mathrm{tok}}=H(\pi_{t})=H_{\mathrm{str}}+H_{\mathrm{hom}}, where HhomH_{\mathrm{hom}} is the expected entropy of the token given its string.

Existing designs.

Prior schemes fall into three families (Table 1).

Filters restrict πt\pi_{t} to a subset of candidates so that the text parses uniquely. Basic drops every candidate whose string prefixes another candidate’s (Nozaki and Murawaki, 2022). MWIS keeps a maximum-weight prefix-free subset (Yan et al., 2023). Stepwise verification keeps the candidates whose addition leaves the history canonically tokenized (Yan and Murawaki, 2025). Dropping any positive-mass candidate changes πt\pi_{t}, so the stegotext deviates from ordinary sampling.

SyncPool groups prefix-related candidates into pools, encodes the pool, and draws the member with shared randomness (Qi et al., 2025). Its law is exact, but the coder sees only pool masses. When one short token is a prefix of many candidates, the pools merge, and capacity collapses as the vocabulary grows (Yan et al., 2026a).

Multi-history designs evaluate the model on several tokenizations of the text, so that the coder can work on strings rather than tokens (Feng et al., 2025). They can be exact and use nearly all of HstrH_{\mathrm{str}}, but each step costs more than one model call.

3 Rare Ambiguity, Real Cost

We fix one generation step and drop the step index. Let pp be the string law at this step (Section 2) and S=supp⁡pS=\operatorname{supp}p. Strings are compared byte by byte: v≺wv\prec w means that vv is a proper prefix of ww.

Definition 1 (Prefix forest).

The parent of w∈Sw\in S is its longest proper prefix in SS, if one exists. This relation makes SS a forest. Its roots ℛ\mathcal{R} are the strings with no proper prefix in SS, and ch⁡(v)\operatorname{ch}(v) denotes the children of vv. A node is a string with at least one child. The mass of vv is M⁡(v)=∑w∈S,v⪯wp⁡(w)M(v)=\sum_{w\in S,\,v\preceq w}p(w), and the stop probability of a node is qv=p⁡(v)/M⁡(v)q_{v}=p(v)/M(v).

Drawing V∼pV\sim p is the same as walking down the forest. The walk enters the tree of root rr with probability M⁡(r)M(r). At each node vv it reaches, it stops with probability qvq_{v}; otherwise it moves to child cc with probability M⁡(c)/(M⁡(v)−p⁡(v))M(c)/(M(v)-p(v)). The chain rule of entropy, applied to this walk, splits the string entropy into three parts.

Lemma 1 (Grouping).

H⁡(p)=Hroot+Hbranch+HstopH(p)=H_{\mathrm{root}}+H_{\mathrm{branch}}+H_{\mathrm{stop}}, where

Hroot\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{root}} =H⁡((M⁡(r))r∈ℛ),\displaystyle=H\bigl((M(r))_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\bigr),
Hstop\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{stop}} =∑v​nodeM⁡(v)​h2​(qv),\displaystyle=\textstyle\sum_{v\ \mathrm{node}}M(v)\,h_{2}(q_{v}),
Hbranch\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{branch}} =∑v​node(M⁡(v)−p⁡(v))​H​(γv),\displaystyle=\textstyle\sum_{v\ \mathrm{node}}\bigl(M(v)-p(v)\bigr)\,H(\gamma_{v}),

γv=(M⁡(c)/(M⁡(v)−p⁡(v)))c∈ch⁡(v)\gamma_{v}=\bigl(M(c)/(M(v)-p(v))\bigr)_{c\in\operatorname{ch}(v)} is the child law at vv, and h2h_{2} is the binary entropy.

HrootH_{\mathrm{root}} is the entropy of choosing a tree, HstopH_{\mathrm{stop}} the entropy of the stop/go decisions, and HbranchH_{\mathrm{branch}} the entropy of choosing a child. Together with Htok=Hstr+HhomH_{\mathrm{tok}}=H_{\mathrm{str}}+H_{\mathrm{hom}} (Section 2), the lemma gives the ladder Hroot≤Hstr−Hstop≤Hstr≤HtokH_{\mathrm{root}}\leq H_{\mathrm{str}}-H_{\mathrm{stop}}\leq H_{\mathrm{str}}\leq H_{\mathrm{tok}}, and Figure 1 shows HstopH_{\mathrm{stop}} on one step.

We now measure how much entropy each term carries under ordinary sampling on our three C4 continuation benchmarks: English with Llama-3.2-3B, Chinese with Qwen3-4B-Base, and Japanese with llm-jp-3-3.7b (50 prompts ×\times 64 tokens per setting; protocol in Section 5.1).

Ambiguous text is rare, yet the stop entropy is paid at every step.

In the texts of Section 5, which follow ordinary sampling, at most 11 tokens in 1,000 differ from canonical retokenization (Yan and Murawaki, 2025) in any setting (Appendix F; see also Geh et al., 2024; Chatzi et al., 2025). A single-history receiver cannot exploit this rarity. Whenever the candidate pool contains a string vv and a proper extension of it, the scheme must decide at step tt whether the token ends at vv, before the text that would settle the question exists. The resulting stop entropy takes 7.2–9.0% of HstrH_{\mathrm{str}} in every setting (Figure 2). The cost lies in the candidate pool, not in the realized text.

SyncPool’s collapse comes from a handful of hub tokens.

SyncPool’s coder sees only the tree masses M⁡(r)M(r), so it forgoes all of HbranchH_{\mathrm{branch}}, and a few short hub tokens that prefix thousands of others make the trees large. In Llama-3.2-3B, most word tokens begin with a space. Once the bare space token enters the pool, its tree takes in every space-prefixed word: from k=16k=16 to the full vocabulary, the largest tree at each step holds on average 62% to 88% of the probability, the space alone produces 62–89% of HbranchH_{\mathrm{branch}}, and SyncPool’s share of HstrH_{\mathrm{str}} falls from 80.4% to 14.1%. In Qwen3-4B-Base, common characters are three-byte strings that are not prefixes of one another, so up to k=1024k=1024 SyncPool keeps 84.2–86.7% of HstrH_{\mathrm{str}}. With the full vocabulary, single-byte tokens for UTF-8 lead bytes such as 0xE5 and 0xE6 enter the pool, and each merges every character that starts with it; SyncPool’s share falls to 40.5%. In llm-jp-3-3.7b, the hubs are the space and the digits for small kk; from k=1024k=1024 on, byte-fallback tokens for the lead bytes 0xE3, shared by all kana, and 0xE5 join them, and at the full vocabulary 0xE3 alone produces 31% of HbranchH_{\mathrm{branch}}. SyncPool’s share falls gradually, from 85.8% at k=16k=16 to 35.5% with the full vocabulary.

Byte and whitespace hubs inflate HbranchH_{\mathrm{branch}}; lexical prefixes set HstopH_{\mathrm{stop}}.

Weighted by the probability M⁡(v)M(v) of reaching them, 92%, 88% and 87% of nodes on Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen3-4B-Base and llm-jp-3-3.7b have qv<0.1q_{v}<0.1 or qv≥0.9q_{v}\geq 0.9 at the full vocabulary. Multi-byte character prefixes sit near qv=0q_{v}=0: the model almost never stops mid-character, so the top single-byte UTF-8 lead tokens alone contribute 58% and 56% of HbranchH_{\mathrm{branch}} on Chinese and Japanese at the full vocabulary, while no single-byte lead token ranks among the top ten contributors to HstopH_{\mathrm{stop}}. Even the bare space on English, whose own tree carries mean mass M⁡(␣)≈0.76M(\text{{\textvisiblespace}})\approx 0.76, produces 62% of HbranchH_{\mathrm{branch}} yet only 9% of HstopH_{\mathrm{stop}}. The rest of HstopH_{\mathrm{stop}} spreads across complete forms that can either end a token or take a continuation (at most 9% from any single node): function words, stems and punctuation on English (␣a, ␣the, .), single-character morphemes and punctuation on Chinese (de, shi, zhong), and case or topic particles on Japanese (no, ni, to, de, o, wa, ga) that also begin compound particles. Coding only the roots forfeits a whole subtree per hub; coin projection pays only at uncertain token boundaries, so HstopH_{\mathrm{stop}} stays at 7.2–9.0% of HstrH_{\mathrm{str}} while HbranchH_{\mathrm{branch}} rises from 4–11% to 51–77%.

Dropping hubs recovers capacity only by giving up exactness.

Deleting the nodes with qv<0.05q_{v}<0.05 before running SyncPool (hub-drop) leaves the coder 82.0%, 84.3% and 83.3% of HstrH_{\mathrm{str}} on the three models at the full vocabulary. For every model, kk and threshold τ∈{0.01,0.05,0.1,0.2}\tau\in\{0.01,0.05,0.1,0.2\}, this stays below coin projection’s budget, and the law is no longer that of ordinary sampling.

4 Coin Projection

4.1 Construction

Coin projection fixes every stop/go decision in advance with shared randomness and leaves the coder only the choices of root and child.

Definition 2 (Coin projection).

Let c=(cv)v​nodec=(c_{v})_{v\ \mathrm{node}} with cv∈{0,1}c_{v}\in\{0,1\} be stop coins. A string v∈Sv\in S survives if ca=0c_{a}=0 for every node a≺va\prec v, and vv is a leaf or cv=1c_{v}=1. The survivor law is

P~c​(v)=M⁡(v)​∏a∈S,a≺vM⁡(a)M⁡(a)−p⁡(a)\tilde{P}_{c}(v)=M(v)\prod_{a\in S,\ a\prec v}\frac{M(a)}{M(a)-p(a)} (1)

if vv survives, and P~c​(v)=0\tilde{P}_{c}(v)=0 otherwise. When the coins are independent with Pr[cv=1]=qv\Pr[c_{v}=1]=q_{v}, P~c\tilde{P}_{c} is the coin projection of pp.

P~c\tilde{P}_{c} is the law of the walk above once the coins have decided where to stop: the walk stops at vv if cv=1c_{v}=1, and otherwise it moves to a child. The denominators are positive because a node has a child of positive probability.

Proposition 1 (Coin projection is exact and spends all but the stop entropy).

For every coin vector cc:

  1. (a)

    the survivors form a prefix antichain;

  2. (b)

    for every root rr, the survivors in the tree of rr carry total probability M⁡(r)M(r) under P~c\tilde{P}_{c}.

Over independent coins:

  1. (c)

    𝔼c​P~c=p\mathbb{E}_{c}\,\tilde{P}_{c}=p;

  2. (d)

    𝔼c​H​(P~c)=H⁡(p)−Hstop\mathbb{E}_{c}\,H(\tilde{P}_{c})=H(p)-H_{\mathrm{stop}}.

Part (a) holds because a surviving node stopped, so none of its extensions survives. Part (b) holds because the walk entering root rr always ends at a survivor of that tree. For (c), vv survives with probability ∏a≺v(1−qa)⋅qv\prod_{a\prec v}(1-q_{a})\cdot q_{v} (with qv=1q_{v}=1 for a leaf), and this product cancels the product in Equation 1. For (d), given cc, the walk randomizes only over roots and over children at nodes it passes, and node vv is passed with expected probability M⁡(v)−p⁡(v)M(v)-p(v). Appendix A gives the full proofs.

Parsing.

Figure 3 shows one step, and Algorithm 1 in Appendix D gives it at both ends as pseudocode. The unread text starts with the true string. Any other survivor that is also a prefix of the unread text would be comparable with the true string, which part (a) rules out. The receiver therefore finds the string without lookahead, and it calls the model only on the true token history.

Relation to SyncPool.

SyncPool partitions the candidates into the connected components of the prefix relation, which are exactly the trees of the prefix forest. It feeds the coder the tree masses and then draws the member from the chosen tree with shared randomness. By part (b), merging each tree’s survivors turns P~c\tilde{P}_{c} into this input.

Corollary 1 (Coin refines SyncPool for every coin vector).

For every coin vector cc, SyncPool’s coder input is a coarsening of P~c\tilde{P}_{c}. Hence H⁡(P~c)≥HrootH(\tilde{P}_{c})\geq H_{\mathrm{root}} for every cc, and 𝔼c​H​(P~c)−Hroot=Hbranch\mathbb{E}_{c}H(\tilde{P}_{c})-H_{\mathrm{root}}=H_{\mathrm{branch}}.

4.2 No single-history scheme does better

We now show that no exact, zero-error scheme that keeps a single token history can spend more than H⁡(p)−HstopH(p)-H_{\mathrm{stop}} per step, and that essentially only coin projection spends exactly this much.

Definition 3 (Single-history exact schemes).

Sender and receiver share a key KK, a prompt and a public truncation rule. The message mm is uniform and independent of KK. For each step tt, let the coder input PtK(⋅∣x<t)P^{K}_{t}(\cdot\mid x_{<t}) be the conditional law of the token XtX_{t} given KK and the history X<t=x<tX_{<t}=x_{<t}. We model the channel as a stream: once the message is embedded, the sender keeps sampling, and the receiver may read as far ahead as it likes. A scheme belongs to the class if it has the following four properties for every language model.

  1. (i)

    Exact: the token sequence has the law of ordinary sampling.

  2. (ii)

    Online: PtKP^{K}_{t} depends on the model only through its outputs on prefixes of the history.

  3. (iii)

    Single-history receiver: the receiver determines X1,X2,…X_{1},X_{2},\dots in order, and before it has determined XtX_{t} it calls the model only on prefixes of X<tX_{<t}.

  4. (iv)

    Zero error: the receiver always recovers the token sequence.

The class lets the receiver postpone every decision as long as it likes, and lets the sender constrain later steps in any way that (i) permits. The stream model only helps the receiver; it sets aside where a finite text ends, which a scheme could in principle use as a side channel and none of the compared schemes does. SyncPool and coin projection belong to the class; Basic, MWIS, Stepwise and hub-drop violate (i), and multi-history designs (iii).

Theorem 1 (A single history forces antichains).

Assume that the vocabulary has a token for every single byte; byte-level BPE and SentencePiece with byte fallback both do. In every scheme that satisfies (i)–(iv) over all full-support language models, for every key, step and history of positive probability, the support of PtKP^{K}_{t} has at most one token per string, and its strings form a prefix antichain.

The proof in Appendix A constructs a full-support model under which the two candidates emit the same text with positive probability, so one history cannot separate them.

Theorem 2 (The stop-entropy bound).

Let κ\kappa be a random variable, and let (Pκ)(P_{\kappa}) be string laws with 𝔼κ​Pκ=p\mathbb{E}_{\kappa}P_{\kappa}=p such that every supp⁡Pκ\operatorname{supp}P_{\kappa} is a prefix antichain. If X|κ∼PκX\mid\kappa\sim P_{\kappa}, then I⁡(X,κ)≥HstopI(X;\kappa)\geq H_{\mathrm{stop}}, or equivalently

𝔼κ​H​(Pκ)≤H⁡(p)−Hstop.\mathbb{E}_{\kappa}H(P_{\kappa})\ \leq\ H(p)-H_{\mathrm{stop}}. (2)

Equality holds if and only if the following laws do not depend on κ\kappa: the law of the root, and, at every node, the law of the child given that XX passes the node. In that case, every PκP_{\kappa} is a survivor law (1), and along every root-to-leaf chain the first stop has the same law as under independent coins. In other words, PκP_{\kappa} is the coin projection up to how the stop decisions of incomparable nodes are coupled.

Proof sketch.

Write XX as a sequence of decisions along the forest: the root, then stop or go at each node reached, then the child. The chain rule expands I⁡(X,κ)I(X;\kappa) into one nonnegative term per decision. Given κ\kappa, the stop/go decision at a reached node vv is deterministic: if v∈supp⁡Pκv\in\operatorname{supp}P_{\kappa}, the antichain property excludes every extension of vv, so the walk stops; otherwise it goes. This decision is reached with probability M⁡(v)M(v) and has marginal entropy h2​(qv)h_{2}(q_{v}), so its term equals M⁡(v)​h2​(qv)M(v)\,h_{2}(q_{v}). Summing over nodes gives HstopH_{\mathrm{stop}}. Root and child terms vanish exactly when their laws ignore κ\kappa. ∎

On the prefix comparability graph GG of SS, minκ⁡I⁡(X,κ)\min_{\kappa}I(X;\kappa) over independent-set mixtures is Körner’s (1973) graph entropy H⁡(G,p)H(G,p), which satisfies H⁡(p)=H⁡(G,p)+H⁡(G¯,p)H(p)=H(G,p)+H(\bar{G},p) because GG is trivially perfect (Csiszár et al., 1990). Theorem 2 gives H⁡(G,p)=HstopH(G,p)=H_{\mathrm{stop}}, realizes the one-shot split via (1), and characterizes all optimal couplings, such as one coin per tree depth (Appendix A).

Corollary 2 (Budget of single-history schemes).

For every scheme of the class and every TT, the first TT tokens carry at most

I(m;X1:T∣K)≤∑t≤T𝔼[Hstr(pt)−Hstop(pt)]I(m;X_{1:T}\mid K)\leq\textstyle\sum_{t\leq T}\mathbb{E}\bigl[H_{\mathrm{str}}(p_{t})-H_{\mathrm{stop}}(p_{t})\bigr]

bits about the message, where ptp_{t} is the string law at step tt. By zero error, the receiver recovers X1:TX_{1:T} from the text, so this is also what the text reveals about the message. Coin projection meets every per-step bound with equality, so an entropy-efficient coder on top of it loses only the coder’s own overhead. Exceeding the bound requires calling the model off the true history, or giving up exactness or zero error for some model.

The proof applies Theorem 1 and then Theorem 2 at every step (Appendix A).

Remark 1 (Filters that ignore the key).

Let w∗w^{\ast} be the largest mass p⁡(A)p(A) of a prefix antichain AA. Every key-independent law p¯\bar{p} on a prefix antichain AA has KL(p¯∥p)≥−logp(A)≥−logw∗\mathrm{KL}(\bar{p}\,\|\,p)\geq-\log p(A)\geq-\log w^{\ast}, and renormalizing pp on a heaviest antichain, as MWIS does, attains both bounds. Since w∗<1w^{\ast}<1 whenever two candidates in a prefix relation have positive mass, an exact single-history scheme needs a key-dependent antichain, as in coin projection.

4.3 Implementation

Static prefix table.

For each tokenizer we precompute all proper byte-prefix pairs after merging homographs (458k, 519k and 246k pairs; Table 5). To support any top-kk subset S⊆𝒱S\subseteq\mathcal{V} without rebuilding tree pointers, each step masks pairs in SS and sums masses in O⁡(|S|+#​live pairs)O(|S|+\#\text{live pairs}) time (O⁡(|S|)O(|S|) on a fixed vocabulary); all step coins come from one stream expansion (Appendix E).

Determinism and coders.

The projection runs on the CPU in float64 with a fixed reduction order, so both ends compute the same P~\tilde{P} bit for bit. It only changes the distribution handed to the coder, so the coders of Section 2 accept P~\tilde{P} unchanged.

5 Experiments

5.1 Setup

Models and data.

We evaluate one base model per language on C4 continuations (Raffel et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2021): Llama-3.2-3B on English (128k byte-BPE; Grattafiori et al., 2024), Qwen3-4B-Base on Chinese (152k byte-BPE; Yang et al., 2025), and llm-jp-3-3.7b on Japanese (100k byte-fallback SentencePiece; LLM-jp et al., 2024). As in Yan and Murawaki (2025), contexts are the first 10 words on English and 10 characters on Chinese and Japanese, excluding replacement characters.

Protocol.

We sample up to 512 tokens at temperature 1 with k∈{16,64,256,1024,4096}k\in\{16,64,256,1024,4096\} or the full vocabulary, masking special tokens, for 128-bit uniform messages (Appendix E gives k=64,1024k=64,1024 and unfinished counts). All methods use the arithmetic coder of Yan and Murawaki (2025) and matched receivers: Native and Stepwise retokenize canonically (Native falls back to standalone text if prompt tokens change); Basic and MWIS parse the conflict-free pool; SyncPool parses the pool root and draws the member with shared randomness; coin projection parses the unique survivor; and hub-drop drops nodes with qv<0.05q_{v}<0.05 before SyncPool. Contexts, messages and keys are paired across methods and kk (100 per cell; filters to 40964096).

The channel.

The receiver gets only the Unicode text; completing a split multi-byte character took at most 2 extra tokens. Every method runs its official algorithm on byte prefixes without tokenization clean-up (Appendix E).

Metrics.

We report the extraction failure rate (messages not recovered bit for bit); bits per token (BPT) and utilization (message bits over summed full-model entropy along the text), totaled per cell; security divergence KLsec\mathrm{KL}_{\mathrm{sec}} (per-step KL of the key-averaged coder law from top-kk sampling); and step time.

5.2 Main results

Coin projection removes SyncPool’s collapse.

SyncPool and coin projection both match ordinary sampling and recovered every completed message (Table 2), but at the full vocabulary SyncPool’s utilization fell to 12.9% on English, 43.3% on Chinese and 33.3% on Japanese, whereas coin projection kept 88.1%, 93.6% and 89.5%. On Chinese with k≤1024k\leq 1024 both stayed close (Section 3): common characters are disjoint three-byte strings.

What remains is the stop entropy.

Native and Stepwise hand the coder almost the whole law. Across models and kk, coin projection’s utilization reached a median 92% of Native’s and 93% of Stepwise’s, matching the 91–93% of HstrH_{\mathrm{str}} left after HstopH_{\mathrm{stop}} (Sections 3 and B), the price of single-history exactness (Theorem 2). Native failed instead: 13, 10 and 25 lost messages on English, Chinese and Japanese decoded to wrong bits without raising an error (Appendix F). Regenerating texts that fail retokenization shifts the law by up to −log⁡(1−r)-\log(1-r) nats per message (rr: 3–8% at 128 bits, 13–40% at 1,024; Appendix G).

Filters trade security for capacity.

Basic drops every internal node of the prefix forest and shifts mass to the leaves, pushing utilization above one at up to 1.48 nats per step. MWIS keeps a heaviest prefix-free set and achieves the smallest divergence among key-independent prefix-free laws (Remark 1); at small kk its utilization approached coin projection’s. Neither MWIS nor Stepwise is exact (.102 and .0035 nats per step on English at k=4096k=4096; .042 for Stepwise on Chinese at k=256k=256), nor is hub-drop (.0059 on English at the full vocabulary). Summed over TT tokens, per-step KL equals the sequence divergence and bounds the text divergence seen by a warden.

5.3 Does the decomposition predict the gain?

By Proposition 1(d) and Corollary 1, the coder budgets of coin projection and SyncPool stand in the ratio (Hstr−Hstop)/Hroot=1+Hbranch/Hroot(H_{\mathrm{str}}-H_{\mathrm{stop}})/H_{\mathrm{root}}=1+H_{\mathrm{branch}}/H_{\mathrm{root}}, which needs only forward passes of ordinary sampling. Figure 4 compares this ratio with the measured ratio of utilizations, and the points follow the diagonal over a sixfold range. The predicted gain rises from 1.14 to 6.46 on English and from 1.07 to 2.60 on Japanese, where lead bytes enter the pool gradually. On Chinese it reaches only 1.15 at k=4096k=4096, where characters form separate roots, and jumps to 2.27 at the full vocabulary, where single-byte UTF-8 prefixes enter the pool. Points off the diagonal lie above it, so the prediction is conservative. Cell utilization is a harmonic mean over messages, and SyncPool’s varies more than coin projection’s (CV up to 0.54 vs. 0.16); with per-message means, the average deviation drops from 4.9% to 3.9% with both signs (Appendix C).

5.4 Computational cost

On our static prefix-pair table (Section 4.3), coin projection took 12.4 ms per step at k=4096k=4096 and 28.0 ms at full vocabulary on English, vs. 17.8 ms for the forward pass (Table 8, Appendix E). While a heaviest prefix antichain admits an O⁡(|S|)O(|S|) tree DP, we ran Yan and Murawaki’s (2025) solver for MWIS alongside Stepwise (39.1 and 112.8 ms at k=4096k=4096).

6 Related Work

Tokenization ambiguity in steganography.

Beyond Section 2, Yan et al. (2024) verify candidates against the history, Yan and Murawaki (2025) measure inconsistency rates and note the lack of theory, and Yan et al. (2026a) list high capacity under provable security as open. ReTokSync (Wang et al., 2026) resets the coder on ambiguous steps and fixes residual errors over a side channel; TI-StegoAlign (Zhou et al., 2026) post-trains the model against inconsistent outputs and alters the base law. Alkaid (Cao et al., 2026b) treats ambiguity as an edit error at ≈0.2\approx 0.2 bits per token and nonzero failure risk; without edits, ambiguity is removable error-free. Bauer et al. (2024) report tokenization failures in deployed messaging.

From tokens to bytes and graph entropy.

Prefix masses M⁡(v)M(v) and stop probabilities qvq_{v} appear in converting token models to byte or character laws (Loula et al., 2025; Vieira et al., 2025a; Phan et al., 2025; Hayase et al., 2026) and marginalizing tokenizations (Cao and Rimell, 2021); those methods query several tokenizations, whereas coin projection uses shared randomness on one history and realizes a perfect-graph entropy split (Körner, 1973; Csiszár et al., 1990).

7 Conclusion

A single-history receiver must pay the stop entropy HstopH_{\mathrm{stop}} of ambiguous word and morpheme prefixes in the candidate pool, even when ambiguous text is rare; coin projection pays nothing more and preserves whitespace and UTF-8 hub trees for the coder. On English, Chinese and Japanese, it keeps 91–93% of string entropy even at full vocabularies, giving 2.16–6.85×\times SyncPool’s utilization at zero divergence and zero error.

Limitations

Scope of the bound.

Our bound covers online schemes that keep a single history, never fail, and are exact across all full-support language models (Appendix A). It is the price of this universality across models: a scheme that needs exactness only for models whose non-canonical continuations are rare can pay less (Appendix A). In the extreme, a model that places no mass on non-canonical encodings (Vieira et al., 2025b) makes canonical retokenization exact; making a deployed model canonical, however, changes the law that the stegotext must match. Likewise, relaxing token-level exactness to text-level exactness across full-support models does not raise the single-history budget when the sender is online along a single history (Appendix A); exceeding Hstr−HstopH_{\mathrm{str}}-H_{\mathrm{stop}} via text-level exactness requires the sender to query alternative tokenizations of the text.

Capacity.

Coin projection still pays HstopH_{\mathrm{stop}}, 7.2–9.0% of the entropy in our measurements. Exceeding it requires multiple histories or a nonzero divergence.

Computation.

Like every provably secure scheme, the receiver needs the model. With the full vocabulary, our CPU implementation of the projection takes 28.0 ms per step on English, against 17.8 ms for the forward pass of the 3B model. Bit-exact agreement between sender and receiver relies on a fixed computation order.

Finite precision.

Exactness here is a property of the law handed to the coder. The arithmetic coder still rounds probabilities, and Cao et al. (2026a) detect arithmetic-coding and Meteor stegotext from the low-probability tokens that rounding removes. This concerns the coder rather than disambiguation and applies equally to every method we compare; coin projection can feed any coder that closes this gap. Our divergence is likewise a per-step quantity: every compared method stops the text once the message is complete, and we do not analyze what the resulting length reveals.

Experimental scale.

Our models have 3–4B parameters, and we cover three languages and two tokenizer families. Larger models of these families share their tokenizers, so the prefix forest and its hub tokens stay the same and only the next-token law changes; the forward-only prediction of Section 5.3 estimates the gain for such a model from its forward passes, but we have not measured extraction end to end beyond 4B.

Ethics Statement

Steganography protects private communication, and it can also hide harmful content. Our method does not make stegotext easier to produce than existing provably secure schemes; it makes extraction reliable. We will release code for research use.

The proofs of (c) and (d) use the coins only through the probability that the first stop along each path occurs at a given string. Any coupling that preserves these probabilities gives the same results.

A.3 Corollary 1

Two strings of SS are comparable only if they share a root, and every string is comparable with its root. Hence the connected components of the prefix relation on SS, which are SyncPool’s groups, are exactly the trees of FF. SyncPool feeds the coder the group masses (M⁡(r))r(M(r))_{r}. By Proposition 1(b), this is the image of P~c\tilde{P}_{c} under the map that sends each survivor to its root. A deterministic map cannot increase entropy, so H⁡(P~c)≥HrootH(\tilde{P}_{c})\geq H_{\mathrm{root}} for every cc. Finally, 𝔼c​H​(P~c)−Hroot=Hbranch\mathbb{E}_{c}H(\tilde{P}_{c})-H_{\mathrm{root}}=H_{\mathrm{branch}} by Proposition 1(d). ∎

A.4 Theorem 1

Model.

A language model maps every token sequence, prompt included, to a law over the vocabulary. The receiver is deterministic given the key KK, the prompt and the stream YY, and it accesses the model as an oracle. By (iii), it outputs decisions X^1,X^2,…\hat{X}_{1},\hat{X}_{2},\dots in order. Before it outputs X^t\hat{X}_{t}, it queries only sequences (prompt,X^<s)(\text{prompt},\hat{X}_{<s}) with s≤ts\leq t. By induction, X^t\hat{X}_{t} is a function of KK, YY and the model’s answers on these sequences.

Proof.

Suppose for contradiction that at some step tt, history hh and distinct tokens x≠x′x\neq x^{\prime} with β⁡(x′)=β⁡(x)⋅s\beta(x^{\prime})=\beta(x)\cdot s (ss possibly empty), the event E={X<t=h,x,x′∈suppPtK(⋅∣h)}E=\{X_{<t}=h,\ x,x^{\prime}\in\operatorname{supp}P^{K}_{t}(\cdot\mid h)\} has positive probability under a full-support model LM0\mathrm{LM}_{0}. Then there exist a,c>0a,c>0 and a measurable set G0G_{0} of keys with μ(G0)=Pr[K∈G0]>0\mu(G_{0})=\Pr[K\in G_{0}]>0 such that for every κ∈G0\kappa\in G_{0}, Pr⁡[X<t=h∣K=κ]≥a\Pr[X_{<t}=h\mid K=\kappa]\geq a and Ptκ​(x∣h),Ptκ​(x′∣h)≥cP^{\kappa}_{t}(x\mid h),P^{\kappa}_{t}(x^{\prime}\mid h)\geq c. Fix an infinite byte string gg and positive numbers (δj)j≥1(\delta_{j})_{j\geq 1} in (0,12)(0,\tfrac{1}{2}) with ∑j=1∞δj≤14​a​c​μ​(G0)\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\delta_{j}\leq\frac{1}{4}ac\,\mu(G_{0}). Define a full-support model LM∗\mathrm{LM}^{\ast} that agrees with LM0\mathrm{LM}_{0} on every sequence extending neither (prompt,h,x)(\text{prompt},h,x) nor (prompt,h,x′)(\text{prompt},h,x^{\prime}). Along the unique single-byte token path spelling s⋅gs\cdot g after (prompt,h,x)(\text{prompt},h,x), its jj-th step puts mass 1−δj1-\delta_{j} on the jj-th byte token of s⋅gs\cdot g and splits δj\delta_{j} uniformly over the other |𝒱|−1|\mathcal{V}|-1 tokens (and puts uniform weights off that path). After (prompt,h,x′)(\text{prompt},h,x^{\prime}), it does the same for gg. Because x≠x′x\neq x^{\prime}, neither sequence extends the other, so LM∗\mathrm{LM}^{\ast} is well defined and strictly positive everywhere.

Step tt is unchanged. LM∗\mathrm{LM}^{\ast} agrees with LM0\mathrm{LM}_{0} on every prefix of (prompt,h)(\text{prompt},h). By (ii), the coder inputs up to step tt on prefixes of hh are identical under LM∗\mathrm{LM}^{\ast}, so every κ∈G0\kappa\in G_{0} still satisfies Pr∗[X<t=h,Xt=u∣K=κ]≥ac\Pr^{\ast}[X_{<t}=h,X_{t}=u\mid K=\kappa]\geq ac for u∈{x,x′}u\in\{x,x^{\prime}\}.

Thus X^t\hat{X}_{t} takes one value while XtX_{t} takes both xx and x′x^{\prime} with positive probability, contradicting (iv). ∎

Remarks and text-level exactness.

The sender may constrain later steps however it likes, as long as it calls the model only on prefixes of the emitted history (ii); exactness across full-support models removes that freedom on the two branches. The bound is therefore the price of exactness across models. A scheme that needs exactness only for models whose non-canonical continuations are rare can pay less: a key keeping both vv and an extension ww can forbid, at the next step, tokens continuing vv into ww, while keys cutting at vv compensate for the forbidden mass; on LM∗\mathrm{LM}^{\ast} such compensation fails. Moreover, if the sender satisfies (ii), replacing token-level exactness (i) by text-level exactness (the byte stream has the same law as under ordinary sampling for every full-support model) leaves the class unchanged. Indeed, fix any model LM0\mathrm{LM}_{0}, history hh of positive probability and token xx; draw independent random infinite byte strings g(u)g^{(u)} for every token uu, and let LM∗\mathrm{LM}^{\ast} agree with LM0\mathrm{LM}_{0} on prefixes of (prompt,h)(\text{prompt},h) while concentrating mass 1−δj1-\delta_{j} along g(u)g^{(u)} after each (prompt,h,u)(\text{prompt},h,u). By (ii), Pr∗⁡[X<t=h,Xt=x]\Pr^{\ast}[X_{<t}=h,X_{t}=x] is unchanged, and no other branch u≠xu\neq x queries g(x)g^{(x)}, so almost surely over g(x)g^{(x)} only (h,x)(h,x) can emit prompt⋅β⁡(h)⋅β⁡(x)⋅g(x)\text{prompt}\cdot\beta(h)\cdot\beta(x)\cdot g^{(x)} with positive probability; letting ∑jδj→0\sum_{j}\delta_{j}\to 0 forces Pr⁡[X<t=h,Xt=x]=π0​(h,x)\Pr[X_{<t}=h,X_{t}=x]=\pi_{0}(h,x) for every (h,x)(h,x), recovering token-level exactness (i). Zero error in (iv) concerns the tokens, not only the message, because the receiver needs the true history to compute later coder inputs; at the final step of a finite message, merging two candidates with the same message value gains at most that single step’s stop entropy.

Couplings and graph entropy.

Our implementation draws one independent coin per node via a single stream expansion per step (Appendix E). Sharing coins between incomparable nodes, for example one uniform per tree depth (at most 85, 85 and 15 internal levels on our English, Chinese and Japanese tokenizers), remains optimal by Theorem 2. SyncPool’s member draw is an antichain mixture too, but its child choice depends on the shared randomness; it is therefore strictly below the bound whenever Hbranch>0H_{\mathrm{branch}}>0. In zero-error source coding, min⁡I⁡(X,κ)\min I(X;\kappa) over variables κ\kappa whose conditional supports are independent sets of a graph GG is Körner’s (1973) graph entropy H⁡(G,p)H(G,p). Here GG is the comparability graph of the prefix forest FF, a trivially perfect graph (P4P_{4}- and C4C_{4}-free) whose independent sets are prefix antichains and whose cliques (independent sets of G¯\bar{G}) are chains of FF. Drawing a root r∼Mr\sim M and a child Cv∼γvC_{v}\sim\gamma_{v} at every node vv independently of the stop coins selects a root-to-leaf chain ZZ intersecting the surviving antichain Y=supp⁡P~cY=\operatorname{supp}\tilde{P}_{c} at {X}\{X\}, with Y⟂ZY\perp Z, I⁡(X,Y)=HstopI(X;Y)=H_{\mathrm{stop}}, and I⁡(X,Z)=Hroot+HbranchI(X;Z)=H_{\mathrm{root}}+H_{\mathrm{branch}}. This recovers Csiszár et al.’s (1990) perfect-graph identity H⁡(p)=H⁡(G,p)+H⁡(G¯,p)H(p)=H(G,p)+H(\bar{G},p) in closed form via (1), while Theorem 1 supplies the multi-step streaming reduction that forces single-history schemes onto GG at every step.

Let pA=p(⋅∣A)p_{A}=p(\cdot\mid A). For p¯\bar{p} supported on AA, KL(p¯∥p)=∑x∈Ap¯(x)logp¯​(x)p⁡(x)=KL(p¯∥pA)−logp(A)≥−logp(A)\mathrm{KL}(\bar{p}\|p)=\sum_{x\in A}\bar{p}(x)\log\frac{\bar{p}(x)}{p(x)}=\mathrm{KL}(\bar{p}\|p_{A})-\log p(A)\geq-\log p(A), with equality if and only if p¯=pA\bar{p}=p_{A}; maximizing p⁡(A)p(A) over antichains gives −log⁡w∗-\log w^{\ast}. If two strings u≺vu\prec v both have positive mass, no antichain contains both, so w∗<1w^{\ast}<1. For an exact scheme of the class, Theorem 1 makes every coder input an antichain law, and these laws average to pp. If they did not depend on the key, each would equal pp, whose support is not an antichain. ∎

Key-conditioned divergence.

For any mixture with p¯=𝔼κ​Pκ\bar{p}=\mathbb{E}_{\kappa}P_{\kappa}, 𝔼κKL(Pκ∥p)=𝔼κ∑xPκ(x)logPκ​(x)p¯​(x)+∑xp¯(x)logp¯​(x)p⁡(x)=I(X;κ)+KL(p¯∥p)\mathbb{E}_{\kappa}\mathrm{KL}(P_{\kappa}\|p)=\mathbb{E}_{\kappa}\sum_{x}P_{\kappa}(x)\log\frac{P_{\kappa}(x)}{\bar{p}(x)}+\sum_{x}\bar{p}(x)\log\frac{\bar{p}(x)}{p(x)}=I(X;\kappa)+\mathrm{KL}(\bar{p}\|p). For an exact scheme the second term vanishes, so the coder input under a fixed key differs from pp by HstopH_{\mathrm{stop}} on average under coin projection and by Hbranch+HstopH_{\mathrm{branch}}+H_{\mathrm{stop}} under SyncPool. A warden without the key never observes the key-conditioned law, so this divergence is not a security loss.

Appendix B Numerical Checks of the Theory

We check the finite-domain identities and bounds of Section 4 directly in float64 arithmetic on 300 fixed-seed random prefix forests with 3 to 10 strings over {a,b,c}≤4\{a,b,c\}^{\leq 4}. Table 3 summarizes the residuals:

  • •

    Pointwise subtree conservation (Proposition 1(b) and Corollary 1). Enumerating every stop pattern c∈{0,1}nodesc\in\{0,1\}^{\text{nodes}} of every forest confirms that the survivor probability inside each root tree of rr matches M⁡(r)M(r) to within 2.22×10−162.22\times 10^{-16}, and that H⁡(P~c)≥HrootH(\tilde{P}_{c})\geq H_{\mathrm{root}} holds for every pattern without exception.

  • •

    Stop-entropy upper bound (Theorem 2). Across 6,000 random mixtures (Pκ)(P_{\kappa}) of antichain-supported string laws with arbitrary mixture weights and mean p¯=𝔼κ​Pκ\bar{p}=\mathbb{E}_{\kappa}P_{\kappa}, the largest positive excess 𝔼κ​H​(Pκ)−(H⁡(p¯)−Hstop​(p¯))\mathbb{E}_{\kappa}H(P_{\kappa})-(H(\bar{p})-H_{\mathrm{stop}}(\bar{p})) is 1.11×10−161.11\times 10^{-16}.

  • •

    Couplings versus child randomization (Theorem 2 equality condition). When incomparable nodes at the same tree depth share a single uniform coin, the marginal equals pp to within 10−1210^{-12} and 𝔼κ​H​(P~κ)\mathbb{E}_{\kappa}H(\tilde{P}_{\kappa}) matches H​(p)−Hstop​(p)H(p)-H_{\mathrm{stop}}(p) to within 1.33×10−151.33\times 10^{-15}. By contrast, a SyncPool-style kernel that encodes the root and uses shared randomness to pick the tree member falls short of H​(p)−Hstop​(p)H(p)-H_{\mathrm{stop}}(p) by up to 1.221.22 bits whenever Hbranch>0H_{\mathrm{branch}}>0.

Along the generated texts.

Proposition 1(d) also holds on the language models of Section 5. At every step of every coin-projection message, we record the entropy of the coder input under the coins drawn at that step and the budget Hstr−HstopH_{\mathrm{str}}-H_{\mathrm{stop}} of the same step. Summed over the messages of a cell, the first is 0.997–1.003 times the second in all 18 cells. The arithmetic coder turns this entropy into message bits with an efficiency of 0.97–1.02, measured as message bits divided by the summed entropy of the coder input. Values above one occur because a message ends once the self-information of the chosen tokens reaches 128 bits, and the self-information fluctuates around the entropy. The budget of Corollary 2, not the coder, therefore sets the utilization of coin projection in Table 2.

Appendix C Predicted and Measured Gain

Table 4 compares, for every model and kk, the predicted gain of Figure 4 with two measured ratios of coin projection’s to SyncPool’s utilization: the ratio of their mean per-message utilizations, and the ratio of their totals, which Tables 2 and 4 report. Every message carries 128 bits, so the total utilization of nn messages with utilizations u1,…,unu_{1},\dots,u_{n} is their harmonic mean n/∑iui−1n/\sum_{i}u_{i}^{-1}. A harmonic mean falls further below the arithmetic mean the more its terms spread, and SyncPool’s utilization spreads more between messages than coin projection’s, whose coefficient of variation stays between 0.11 and 0.16. The total ratio is therefore at least the per-message ratio in all 18 cells, and up to 20% above it. Per message, the mean absolute relative deviation |Msg/Pred−1||\text{Msg}/\text{Pred}-1| across the 18 cells is 3.9% (vs. 4.9% for |Total/Pred−1||\text{Total}/\text{Pred}-1|) and at most 9%, in both directions; the prediction also carries the sampling error of the forward passes, which the intervals of Figure 4 omit. The 512-token limit of Table 2 lowers the measured gain further: an unfinished message counts as finished at 512 tokens, which raises the utilization of the method that failed, and on English 16 SyncPool messages and 3 coin-projection messages over all kk were unfinished.

Appendix E Experimental Details

Models, tokenizers and static prefix tables.

Table 5 lists the three base language models and their byte-level vocabulary structures. For each vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V}, we extract the raw byte string β⁡(x)\beta(x) of every token xx: via the byte-level BPE inverse map for Llama-3.2-3B and Qwen3-4B-Base, and via <0xHH> byte-fallback decoding plus replacement of ‘ ‘ (U+2581) by ASCII space for llm-jp-3-3.7b. Special tokens, added control tokens, and tokens with empty byte strings are masked out before the softmax at every step. Tokens with identical non-empty byte strings are merged into a single string key for the prefix forest and resolved after string selection via shared randomness (Algorithm 1, line 9). We precompute all proper byte-prefix pairs (a,d)(a,d) once per tokenizer and store them sorted both by ascending and by descending ancestor byte length; finding the longest live prefix (parent in the forest) or shortest live prefix (tree root) of every candidate in an arbitrary top-kk subset S⊆𝒱S\subseteq\mathcal{V} then requires a single boolean mask over the static pair array and no per-step sorting. On a fixed support such as the full vocabulary, parent pointers are static and a single bottom-up tree pass computes MM and P~c\tilde{P}_{c} in O⁡(|S|)O(|S|) time; we keep the same pair-mask path at every kk so that all settings share identical code.

Corpus and paired design.

We draw prompts from the English, Chinese and Japanese splits of C4 (Raffel et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2021), taking the first 10 words for English and the first 10 characters for Chinese and Japanese as in Yan and Murawaki (2025). Prompts containing the Unicode replacement character U+FFFD (11 out of 1,000 in the Chinese shard, 0 in English and Japanese) are discarded deterministically. For sample index ss, every method and every truncation size k∈{16,64,256,1024,4096,Full}k\in\{16,64,256,1024,4096,\text{Full}\} receives the same prompt, the same 128-bit message msm_{s}, and the same 256-bit secret key KsK_{s}. At step tt, one HMAC​-​SHA256​(Ks,label∥t)\mathrm{HMAC\text{-}SHA256}(K_{s},\text{label}\mathbin{\|}t) call derives a step seed, and one SHAKE​-​256\mathrm{SHAKE\text{-}256} call expands it into all node uniforms as 53-bit IEEE 754 doubles in [0,1)[0,1) (≈1.5\approx 1.5 ms even across all 41,302 internal nodes of Llama-3.2-3B; sharing one uniform per tree depth would need at most 85).

Uncertainty and complete kk grid.

Tables 6 and 7 report the two intermediate truncation sizes (k=64,1024k=64,1024) omitted for width in Table 2, together with every unfinished-message count across all six kk settings. Resampling the messages of each cell (2,000 bootstrap draws), the 95% interval of a cell’s utilization has a half-width of at most 4% of its value (median 2.7%) for every method except SyncPool, whose utilization varies most from message to message (up to 14%). Across all six kk settings, the median ratio of the utilization of coin projection to that of Native is 92% (95% interval 91–93%, paired by message), and to that of Stepwise 93% (92–94%). BPT also depends on the entropy of each method’s own text, so one method can have the higher BPT and the lower utilization in the same cell; SyncPool and coin projection on Chinese at k=256k=256 (BPT 2.542.54 vs. 2.502.50, Util .707.707 vs. .757.757 in Table 2) are an example. Utilization divides by the entropy that each text actually offered and is the measure we compare.

Byte-level channel and UTF-8 completion.

The channel carries only the continuation as a Unicode string. With byte-level tokenizers, the arithmetic coder can resolve all 128 message bits at a token boundary that lies inside a multi-byte UTF-8 character. Whenever the coder interval resolves the message at step tt but the concatenated output bytes are not yet valid UTF-8, the sender continues encoding the same message integer for at most 8 additional steps until the byte stream ends on a valid UTF-8 character boundary. Because these trailing steps encode the same integer, the receiver’s arithmetic decoder replays them without altering the recovered 128-bit message. A text whose bytes are still not valid UTF-8—for example when full-vocabulary byte-level sampling emits an unpaired mid-stream byte—cannot be sent as a Unicode string, so its message counts as unfinished, for every method alike (1 SyncPool text at the full vocabulary on English). At both ends we set clean_up_tokenization_spaces=False; otherwise, HuggingFace’s default decoder rewrites punctuation sequences such as “␣,” and invalidates canonical retokenization even when no tokenization ambiguity occurred.

Baseline implementations and equivalence checks.

To separate algorithmic behavior from string-decoding artifacts, all methods operate on the exact byte-level prefix graph:

  • •

    Basic (Nozaki and Murawaki, 2022), MWIS (Yan et al., 2023), SyncPool (Qi et al., 2025), and Stepwise verification (Yan and Murawaki, 2025) call the official pool-construction functions of Yan and Murawaki (2025) with token strings replaced by exact byte strings β⁡(x)\beta(x). On 24 real language-model states across k∈{16,64,256}k\in\{16,64,256\}, our byte-level builders match the official repository’s candidate sets and weights to within 10−1210^{-12}.

  • •

    Lazy-boundary arithmetic coding (FastAC). The reference ArithmeticCoder of Yan and Murawaki (2025) materializes all |S|+1|S|+1 high-precision Decimal interval boundaries at every step, which becomes prohibitive at full vocabulary (|S|≈1.5×105|S|\approx 1.5\times 10^{5}). Because cumulative float64 probabilities are monotone, only the two interval endpoints surrounding the target message value need to be evaluated in Decimal. Across 60 random 128-bit messages (over 4,000 encoding steps) with ties and sparse weights, FastAC produces the exact same symbol indices and Decimal intervals (low, high) as the reference ArithmeticCoder at every step.

  • •

    Method-matched receivers. The public evaluation script of Yan and Murawaki (2025) applies canonical retokenization to all baselines and draws SyncPool members with an unseeded generator, which artificially inflates extraction failures for Basic, MWIS and SyncPool. In our evaluation, Native and Stepwise use canonical retokenization of prompt+text\text{prompt}+\text{text}, and when this changes the prompt tokens, Native tokenizes the text alone (this recovers 7 Chinese messages; no English message needs it, and with SentencePiece the separate tokenization never matches); Basic and MWIS parse the unique matching byte prefix in the conflict-free pool; SyncPool and hub-drop parse the unique pool root and draw the pool member with the shared step uniform; and coin projection parses the unique surviving prefix in supp⁡P~c\operatorname{supp}\tilde{P}_{c}.

Hardware and timing.

All experiments run on a single workstation with one NVIDIA GPU (12 GB VRAM, bfloat16 model weights, float64 CPU distribution coding and projection). Per-step planning time (ms_plan) measures candidate pool construction or coin projection on the CPU; forward time (ms_fwd) measures the model step with KV caching enabled.

Parallel receivers.

Non-canonical tokenizations are rare (Section 3). A receiver could therefore guess the canonical tokenization, verify it with one block forward pass, and fall back at the first deviation. This works only if sender and receiver run with an identical, fixed computation shape (Yan et al., 2026b; Qi et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026; Qin et al., 2026). The idea applies to every single-history scheme, so we do not use it in our experiments; all methods there decode sequentially.

Appendix F Native Failures and Ambiguity Rates

Across the 1800 Native messages in Table 2 (600 per language), 88 completed messages fail to decode (19 on English, 21 on Chinese and 48 on Japanese; Table 9), and 2 more Japanese messages do not finish within 512 tokens. Every failed extraction falls into one of three disjoint categories:

  • •

    Silent wrong bits (48 of 88, 55%). Every retokenized token lies inside the candidate pool at its step, so the arithmetic decoder terminates cleanly and returns 128 bits that do not match the sender’s message. Without an external integrity tag, the receiver cannot tell that desynchronization occurred and therefore cannot request retransmission. At the full vocabulary, candidate-pool membership never fails, so every Native failure that is not a prompt-boundary merge is silent (3, 2 and 7 on English, Chinese and Japanese).

  • •

    Out-of-pool aborts (26 of 88). Canonical retokenization merges or splits emitted bytes into a token outside the top-kk candidate pool at that step, halting the decoder. These failures shrink as kk grows and vanish at the full vocabulary.

  • •

    Prompt-boundary merges (14 of 88). When the continuation does not begin with a whitespace delimiter, the tokenizer can merge the trailing characters of the prompt with the opening bytes of the continuation. Tokenizing the continuation alone recovers 7 of 12 such cases on Chinese; the remaining 5 Chinese cases and all 9 Japanese cases (where SentencePiece prepends ‘ ’ on standalone strings) remain unrecoverable.

Coin projection, SyncPool, Stepwise, MWIS, Basic and hub-drop all achieve zero extraction errors across every completed message.

Native fails exactly on the affected texts.

All three categories come from one event: canonical retokenization at the receiver does not return the sampled tokens. We retokenize every text that Native, SyncPool and coin projection generate in Table 2, and call a text affected when its canonical tokens after the prompt differ from the sampled ones, or when it merges with the prompt and tokenizing it alone does not restore them. Every affected Native text decodes wrongly, and every other Native text decodes correctly. SyncPool’s and coin projection’s texts are affected too, but their receivers do not retokenize, and they decode correctly.

How rare ambiguity is.

To compare with the measure of Yan and Murawaki (2025), we count the tokens of prompt and text whose byte span is not a span of the other tokenization (their SIT and CIT counts, on byte rather than character spans, so that tokens splitting a multi-byte character are counted too). Over 174,160, 96,441 and 109,490 generated tokens, this gives 2.7, 4.1 and 8.0 tokens per 1,000 on English, Chinese and Japanese, and at most 11 in any setting of method and kk (Section 3).

Appendix G Longer Messages and Sender-Side Rejection

Table 10 repeats the comparison at the full vocabulary with 512- and 1,024-bit messages on 15 contexts per language, with the horizon of Table 2: four tokens per message bit. Coin projection recovers every message it completes. SyncPool’s utilization, which collapses at the full vocabulary, stays at or below .415 in every setting. Native keeps its capacity but fails on exactly its affected texts (Amb; Appendix F); coin projection’s texts contain such tokenizations too and still decode.

Sender-side rejection.

Because most of Native’s failures are silent (Appendix F), a receiver cannot ask for a resend, and asking would need a back channel anyway. The sender can instead retokenize its own text and, on a mismatch, regenerate it with fresh randomness (the receiver must then learn which attempt to decode). This removes the failures but not the divergence. If a message is regenerated with probability rr, the accepted token sequences follow ordinary sampling conditioned on an event of probability 1−r1-r, and this law lies −log⁡(1−r)-\log(1-r) nats from ordinary sampling. By data processing, the law of the text lies at most this far, and in general it differs: a text loses the probability of its non-canonical tokenizations, and texts that merge with the prompt are removed altogether. We estimate rr by the share of affected texts. On Native’s 128-bit messages it is 3.2%, 3.5% and 8.0% on English, Chinese and Japanese (at most 0.03, 0.04 and 0.08 nats per message). On Native’s messages in Table 10, rr is 0–20% at 512 bits and 13–40% at 1,024 bits (up to 0.51 nats per message). Stepwise applies the same idea at every step and pays the per-step divergences of Table 2. Coin projection needs no regeneration and keeps the law of ordinary sampling; what it pays instead is HstopH_{\mathrm{stop}}.

Appendix H Multi-History Schemes

Single-history schemes evaluate the language model only on prefixes of the sender’s emitted token sequence X<tX_{<t}. By Corollary 2, their per-step coder budget cannot exceed Hstr−HstopH_{\mathrm{str}}-H_{\mathrm{stop}}. Multi-history schemes such as LAS (Feng et al., 2025) instead keep several weighted candidate token histories consistent with the visible text and query the model on more than one of them per step. Such schemes are not bound by Corollary 2: in the experiments of Feng et al. (2025), LAS codes nearly all of the entropy of ordinary sampling, whereas a single-history scheme must give up HstopH_{\mathrm{stop}} (7.2–9.0% of HstrH_{\mathrm{str}} across our three models; Figure 2). The price is multiple language-model forward passes per token, whereas coin projection achieves the exact single-history optimum Hstr−HstopH_{\mathrm{str}}-H_{\mathrm{stop}} with one forward pass per token.
